reflection.text:
This was a correct call - unblinded compound anisomycin, PubChem CID 253602, scored as Protein synthesis in both protocol and scientist conclusion (verdict.correct=true). Review approved with no additional experiment requested.

What the evidence got right:

The quantitative atlas was decisive and we weighted it correctly. All 4 acquired wells from 0.1 to 10 uM voted Protein synthesis by NSC/Ljosa 1-NN (per-well similarities 0.559 at 0.1 uM in w_c781542bcf, 0.841 at 0.3 uM in w_e43c4b4845, 0.764 at 1.0 uM in w_8e60c73d1a, 0.775 at 10 uM in w_55e65aedb1; summed similarity 2.939, tally 4/4). e2/e3/e6/e7/e8 captured this unanimously. This outweighs k-neighbour dilution (6/10 Protein synthesis vs 4/10 Microtubule stabilizers in e4, 3/10 plus 1/10 Eg5 in e8) because the protocol uses NSC vote, not k-neighbour plurality.

The phenotype itself was extreme but consistent with that class in this screen: act_mean z=+47.0 at 10 uM (e2) to +58.3 at 1 uM (e3), act_glcm_contrast z=+32.6 to +48.6, act_std z=+31.0, with nuc_form_factor z=-39.7 at high dose. Dose_response trajectory reinforced specificity: nuc_form_factor rho=-1.00 (p=0) in e10 and act_mean rho=+0.80 in e9 across 4 doses, despite n=4 and p=0.2 for act_mean. e6 at 0.1 uM already showed act_mean +5.1 and solidity +5.2, indicating onset then strong escalation at 0.3 uM (act_mean +28.4, e7). That monotonic actin/nuclear dose relationship is why we kept hypotheses at Protein synthesis 0.88 in e11/e12 rather than flipping to cytoskeletal classes.

What was misleading and what we discounted:

The blinded describe_phenotype in e5 was the main distractor: microscopist on 4 fields noted lower density vs DMSO and listed candidates Actin disruptors, Aurora kinase inhibitors (9 observations). Visually this makes sense - a z>+47 actin mean with high contrast looks like an actin drug. We assigned Actin disruptors 0.05 and Aurora 0.04 in hypothesis_history explicitly contradicting them with e4/e8 and e2/e3, which was appropriate. The lower cell count (126 cells at 10 uM vs 264-271 at low doses) could suggest toxicity, but atlas retained tubulin and NSC remained unanimous, so we did not over-interpret viability loss as a separate MoA.

Acquisition choices:

list_available_experiments showed 8 doses and budget for 4 wells (e1). Strategy to acquire high dose first (w_55e65aedb1) then 1 uM, then bracket low end 0.1 and 0.3 uM was efficient. It captured maximal effect and dose-dependency without replicate wells. Limitation: single replicate per dose, no DMSO stats or replicate variance, and no orthogonal assay in-screen. Budget left=0 per review, so no further free analysis could have overturned the decisive vote, but in a real lab we proposed Puromycin SUnSET and phospho-eIF2a/ATF4 as next steps.

What we missed / literature context:

lookup_compound e13/e14 returned no curated ChEMBL mechanisms for anisomycin, so we relied entirely on morphology+atlas. Post-unblinding literature confirms the atlas: PMID 3401749 and PMID 3567595 both title anisomycin as an inhibitor of protein synthesis, and PMID 19286921 describes it the same way; PMID 37275259 provides context on global quantification of newly synthesized proteins for inhibitor-specific effects. We did not have that curated annotation pre-unblinding, but the 4/4 vote compensated. We also did not mechanistically explain why protein synthesis inhibition produced such strong actin texture changes; the second PubMed search "protein synthesis inhibition actin cytoskeleton morphology" returned 676 hits (e16), indicating this downstream actin phenotype is reported, but we made no claim beyond dose-dependent morphology and atlas match.

Lesson: when quantitative NSC is unanimous across a dose range with strong monotonic features, it should dominate qualitative visual candidates, even for extreme actin/nuclear z-scores. Probability 0.88 was calibrated - high confidence but retaining residual uncertainty due to phenotypic mimicry of actin modulators and lack of biochemical confirmation.
